sents.text: Root is the user who can do anything on a Linux machine, and sudo is how you borrow that power for one command.
You'll type it often when you install GPU drivers and tools.
Today: what it does, and how not to hurt yourself with it.
A normal user can work with their own files, but can't change the system.
That's a safety net: mistakes stay small.
Root can install anything, change any file, and delete the whole system with one wrong command.
Put it in front of a command, and that one command runs as root.
Linux asks for your own password, not root's, and only users on an approved list are allowed to use it.
That's much safer than logging in as root and staying there.
Use sudo when you change the system: installing packages with apt, installing GPU drivers, changing system settings, or touching files that root owns.
Don't use it for your own work: pip installs inside your virtual environment, editing your own files, running your Python scripts, or git.
If a command works without sudo, run it without sudo.
